--- title: CVXR Functions author: Anqi Fu and Balasubramanian Narasimhan --- ## Functions Here we describe the functions that can be applied to `CVXR` expressions. `CVXR` uses the function information in this section and the [Disciplined Convex Programming tools](https://dcp.stanford.edu/) to mark expressions with a sign and curvature. ### Operators The infix operators `+`, `-`, `*`, `%*%`, `/` are treated as functions. `+` and `-` are affine functions. `*` and `/` are affine in `CVXR` because `expr1*expr2` and `expr1 %*% expr2` are allowed only when one of the expressions is constant and `expr1/expr2` is allowed only when `expr2` is a scalar constant. #### Comparison operators The comparison operators `==`, `<=`, and `>=` are overloaded to create constraint objects: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x == y # Equality constraint x <= y # Inequality constraint (convex <= concave) x >= y # Inequality constraint (concave >= convex) ``` ::: Note that strict inequalities `<` and `>` are **not** supported, nor is `!=`. #### Semidefinite operators The operators `%>>%` and `%<<%` create positive semidefinite (PSD) and negative semidefinite (NSD) constraints, respectively: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} X %>>% 0 # X is PSD X %<<% 0 # X is NSD ``` ::: ::: {.callout-warning} Beware of operator precedence: `A - B %>>% 0` is parsed as `A - (B %>>% 0)`. Use `(A - B) %>>% 0` instead. ::: #### Boolean operators The operators `&`, `|`, and `!` are overloaded for boolean variables to create logical constraints: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x & y # equivalent to And(x, y) x | y # equivalent to Or(x, y) !x # equivalent to Not(x) ``` ::: #### R math and summary functions `CVXR` overloads many standard R functions so they can be applied directly to expressions: - **Math**: `abs()`, `exp()`, `log()`, `sqrt()`, `cumsum()`, `cummax()`, `cumprod()`, `ceiling()`, `floor()`, `sign()`, `log2()`, `log10()`, `log1p()` - **Summary**: `sum()`, `max()`, `min()`, `prod()`, `mean()` - **Complex**: `Re()`, `Im()`, `Conj()`, `Mod()` - **Masked from base/stats**: `diag()`, `norm()`, `outer()`, `sd()`, `var()`, `power()`, `convolve()` These dispatch to the corresponding `CVXR` atoms (e.g., `abs(x)` calls `Abs`, `sum(x)` calls `SumEntries`). On an expression they follow CVXPY; a masked function given anything that is not an expression is exactly the base R or stats function, called as written. ::: {.callout-note} As of `CVXR` 1.9.1, the trigonometric and hyperbolic functions `sin()`, `cos()`, `tan()`, `sinh()`, `tanh()`, `asinh()`, and `atanh()` are supported as **smooth atoms** for disciplined nonlinear programs (see [Smooth functions for DNLP](#smooth-functions-for-dnlp)); they are *not* part of the convex (DCP) grammar. Other R Math group functions not listed above (e.g., `round()`, `trunc()`) remain **not** supported and produce a clear error message if used on `CVXR` expressions. ::: #### Indexing and slicing All non-scalar expressions can be indexed using the syntax `expr[i, j]`. Indexing is an affine function. The syntax `expr[i]` can be used as a shorthand for `expr[i, 1]` when `expr` is a column vector. Similarly, `expr[i]` is shorthand for `expr[1, i]` when `expr` is a row vector. Non-scalar expressions can also be sliced into using the standard R slicing syntax. For example, `expr[i:j, r]` selects rows `i` through `j` of column `r` and returns a vector. `CVXR` supports advanced indexing using lists of indices or boolean arrays. The semantics are the same as in R. Any time R might return a numeric vector, `CVXR` returns a column vector. #### Transpose The transpose of any expression can be obtained using the syntax `t(expr)`. Transpose is an affine function. #### Power For any `CVXR` expression `expr`, the power operator `expr^p` is equivalent to the function `power(expr, p)`. The exponent argument of `power()` is named `lambda`, as in `stats::power()`. ### Scalar functions A scalar function takes one or more scalars, vectors, or matrices as arguments and returns a scalar. ::: {.cell} ::: #### Norms ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: #### Clarifications The domain $\mathbf{S}^n$ refers to the set of symmetric matrices. The domains $\mathbf{S}^n_+$ and $\mathbf{S}^n_-$ refer to the set of positive semi-definite and negative semi-definite matrices, respectively. Similarly, $\mathbf{S}^n_{++}$ and $\mathbf{S}^n_{--}$ refer to the set of positive definite and negative definite matrices, respectively. For a vector expression `x`, `p_norm(x, 2)` gives the Euclidean norm. For a matrix expression `X`, `cvxr_norm(X, 2)` and `sigma_max(X)` give the spectral norm (largest singular value). With no `axis`, the matrix norms agree with base R's `norm()` and with CVXPY: `cvxr_norm(X, 1)` is the largest absolute column sum and `cvxr_norm(X, Inf)` the largest absolute row sum. The masked `norm(X, type)` accepts base R's types, so `norm(X, "O")`, `norm(X, "I")`, `norm(X, "F")`, `norm(X, "M")` and `norm(X, "2")` mean what they mean in base R. With no `type`, `norm(X)` of an expression is the spectral norm, as in CVXPY; on an ordinary R matrix it is base R's one-norm. Any other `p` on a matrix is an error. For the entrywise norms of a matrix use `norm1(X)` (sum of absolute entries), `cvxr_norm(X, "fro")`, or `p_norm(X, p)`. A row vector is a 1 by n matrix, as in base R. The function `cvxr_norm(X, "fro")` is called the [Frobenius norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_norm#Frobenius_norm) and `cvxr_norm(X, "nuc")` (or `norm_nuc(X)`) the [nuclear norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_norm#Schatten_norms). The nuclear norm can also be defined as the sum of `X`'s singular values. The functions `max_entries` and `min_entries` give the largest and smallest entry, respectively, in a single expression. These functions should not be confused with `max_elemwise` and `min_elemwise` (see [Elementwise functions](#elementwise-functions)). Use `max_elemwise` and `min_elemwise` to find the maximum or minimum of a list of scalar expressions. The function `sum_entries` sums all the entries in a single expression. The built-in R `sum` should be used to add together a list of expressions. For example, the following code sums three expressions: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} expr_sum <- sum(expr1, expr2, expr3) ``` ::: ### Functions along an axis The functions `sum_entries`, `cvxr_norm`, `max_entries`, `min_entries`, `cvxr_mean`, `cvxr_var`, `cvxr_std` and `geo_mean` can be applied along an axis, and accept `keepdims` as in CVXPY. Given an `m` by `n` expression `expr`, the syntax `func(expr, axis=1)` applies `func` to each row, returning a `m` by 1 expression. The syntax `func(expr, axis=2)` applies `func` to each column, returning a 1 by `n` expression. For example, the following code sums along the columns and rows of a matrix variable: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} X <- Variable(c(5, 4)) row_sums <- sum_entries(X, axis=1) # Has size (5, 1) col_sums <- sum_entries(X, axis=2) # Has size (1, 4) ``` ::: Note that the use of `axis` differs from its use in `CVXPY` where `axis=0` implies the rows. In `CVXR`, we align our implementation with the `base::apply` function. The default in most cases is `axis = NULL`, which treats a matrix as one long vector, basically the same as apply with `c(1,2)`. The exceptions are `cumsum()`, `cumprod()` and `cummax()` (and `cumsum_axis()`, `cummax_expr()`), which default to `axis = 2`, down each column, as in CVXPY; `cumsum_axis(x, axis = NULL)` gives all entries in column-major order as a column. ### Elementwise functions {#elementwise-functions} These functions operate on each element of their arguments. For example, if `X` is a 5 by 4 matrix variable, then `abs(X)` is a 5 by 4 matrix expression. `abs(X)[1, 2]` is equivalent to `abs(X[1, 2])`. Elementwise functions that take multiple arguments, such as `max_elemwise` and `multiply`, operate on the corresponding elements of each argument. For example, if `X` and `Y` are both 3 by 3 matrix variables, then `max_elemwise(X, Y)` is a 3 by 3 matrix expression. `max_elemwise(X, Y)[2, 1]` is equivalent to `max_elemwise(X[2, 1], Y[2, 1])`. This means all arguments must have the same dimensions or be scalars, which are promoted. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

As in CVXPY, their value rounds `x` to 4 decimal places first, so `floor(-3e-10)` of an expression is 0, not -1. `sign(x)` of a scalar expression is also quasilinear and, as in CVXPY, is -1 for `x <= 0`, so `sign(0)` of an expression is -1, not 0. ### Vector/matrix functions A vector/matrix function takes one or more scalars, vectors, or matrices as arguments and returns a vector or matrix. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

The `scalarize` functions take a list of `Minimize`/`Maximize` objectives and return one objective, for multi-objective problems. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Function Meaning

````` ::: ::: ### Smooth functions for DNLP {#smooth-functions-for-dnlp} The functions below are **smooth atoms** added in `CVXR` 1.9.1 for [disciplined nonlinear programming](../examples/dnlp/tutorial.qmd) (DNLP). They are twice continuously differentiable but are *not* part of the convex (DCP) grammar, so they may be used only in smooth (possibly nonconvex) problems solved with `psolve(prob, nlp = TRUE)`. | Function | Meaning | Domain | |----------|---------|--------| | `sin(x)`, `cos(x)` | Trigonometric functions | all $x$ | | `tan(x)` | Tangent | $x \in (-\pi/2,\ \pi/2)$ | | `sinh(x)`, `tanh(x)` | Hyperbolic functions | all $x$ | | `asinh(x)` | Inverse hyperbolic sine | all $x$ | | `atanh(x)` | Inverse hyperbolic tangent | $x \in (-1,\ 1)$ | | `normcdf(x)` | Standard normal CDF | all $x$ | | `prod(x)` | Product of entries | all $x$ | | `convolve(x, y)` | 1-D discrete convolution (numpy-style alias for `conv`; on numeric vectors it is `stats::convolve()`) | all $x$ | In a DNLP, elementwise multiplication `x * y` and `quad_form(x, Q)` also become smooth and may take *two* variable arguments (in DCP, `x * y` requires one operand to be constant). Use `is_dnlp(prob)` to check whether a problem satisfies the DNLP grammar (every DCP problem qualifies). For nonconvex DNLPs, `psolve(prob, nlp = TRUE, best_of = n)` runs `n` random restarts, drawing initial points from variable bounds or from a region set with `sample_bounds(x) <- c(low, high)`. See the [DNLP Tutorial](../examples/dnlp/tutorial.qmd). Individual expressions can also be classified directly, mirroring CVXPY's `expr.is_smooth()` family: `is_smooth(e)` is `TRUE` when `e` is twice continuously differentiable, while `is_linearizable_convex(e)` and `is_linearizable_concave(e)` report whether `e` becomes convex (respectively concave) once every smooth subexpression is linearized. For instance, `is_smooth(sin(x))` is `TRUE` and `is_smooth(abs(x))` is `FALSE`, while `is_linearizable_convex(abs(x))` is `TRUE`. These are the per-expression rules that `is_dnlp()` composes over a whole problem. ### Curvature queries `curvature(e)` returns the curvature of an expression as a string, checking, as CVXPY does, in this order: `"CONSTANT"`, `"AFFINE"`, `"CONVEX"`, `"CONCAVE"`, then the log-log curvatures (`"LOG-LOG AFFINE"`, `"LOG-LOG CONVEX"`, `"LOG-LOG CONCAVE"`), then the quasi curvatures (`"QUASILINEAR"`, `"QUASICONVEX"`, `"QUASICONCAVE"`), and `"UNKNOWN"` if none applies. `curvatures(e)` returns every curvature that applies, and `log_log_curvature(e)` returns only the log-log one. `is_diag(x)` reports whether a leaf was declared `diag = TRUE`. Each curvature also has a predicate returning `TRUE` or `FALSE`: `is_constant()`, `is_affine()`, `is_convex()`, `is_concave()`, `is_log_log_affine()`, `is_log_log_convex()`, `is_log_log_concave()`, `is_quasilinear()`, `is_quasiconvex()` and `is_quasiconcave()`. A whole problem is checked with `is_dcp()`, `is_dgp()`, `is_dqcp()`, `is_dpp()` and `is_dnlp()`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- Variable(pos = TRUE) y <- Variable(pos = TRUE) curvature(x * y) # "LOG-LOG AFFINE" curvature(ceiling(Variable())) # "QUASILINEAR" curvatures(sqrt(x)) # "CONCAVE", "LOG-LOG AFFINE", ... log_log_curvature(x + y) # "LOG-LOG CONVEX" ``` ::: ## Session Info ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24) Platform: aarch64-apple-darwin23 Running under: macOS Tahoe 26.6.2 Matrix products: default BLAS: /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/4.6/Resources/lib/libRblas.0.dylib LAPACK: /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/4.6/Resources/lib/libRlapack.dylib; LAPACK version 3.12.1 locale: [1] en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/C/en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8 time zone: America/Los_Angeles tzcode source: internal attached base packages: [1] stats graphics grDevices utils datasets methods base other attached packages: [1] kableExtra_1.4.1 loaded via a namespace (and not attached): [1] vctrs_0.7.3 svglite_2.2.2 cli_3.6.6 knitr_1.52 [5] rlang_1.3.0 xfun_0.61 stringi_1.8.9 otel_0.2.0 [9] textshaping_1.0.5 jsonlite_2.0.0 glue_1.8.1 htmltools_0.5.9 [13] scales_1.4.0 rmarkdown_2.32 evaluate_1.0.5 fastmap_1.2.0 [17] yaml_2.3.12 lifecycle_1.0.5 stringr_1.6.0 compiler_4.6.1 [21] RColorBrewer_1.1-3 htmlwidgets_1.6.4 rstudioapi_0.19.0 systemfonts_1.3.2 [25] farver_2.1.2 digest_0.6.39 viridisLite_0.4.3 R6_2.6.1 [29] dichromat_2.0-1 magrittr_2.0.5 tools_4.6.1 xml2_1.6.0 ``` ::: :::
